fields.title: The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to her life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Elisabeth Elliot’s teaching — that God is sovereign and His love is everlasting, so that the believer may accept whatever He gives, do the next thing, offer every loss back to Him, and find in obedience the only real liberty. Fifteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion to Elisabeth Elliot’s ministry, naming her books for the reader’s own further study.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Elisabeth Elliot, not a book by her. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in fifteen short chapters the teaching for which the missionary, widow, writer and broadcaster is chiefly remembered — the sovereignty and love of God as the ground of everything, the duty of the present moment, suffering that is never wasted, the acceptance of what God gives and the offering of it back to Him, the liberty that is found in obedience, the disciplines of the Christian life, love placed under the lordship of Christ, loneliness, womanhood and the Christian home, the missionary without illusions, the way of the cross, the quiet heart, the questions we bring to God, and thanksgiving in all things. It opens with an account of her life and closes with a conclusion and a guide to her books.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any organisation that holds rights in the writings of Elisabeth Elliot. All descriptions of her teaching are the present author’s own summaries; her books are named only for the reader’s further study, and readers are warmly encouraged to obtain them from their rightful publishers. Nothing of Elisabeth Elliot’s own text is reproduced here — only Scripture, quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, a few lines of older verse and a single sentence of Amy Carmichael’s, all long in the public domain, and Ochorus’s account of what she taught.

Elisabeth Elliot was admired by many and argued with by some, and she would not have wanted a companion that pretended otherwise. This volume tries to honour her by telling plainly what she taught, by noting fairly where faithful Christians have differed from her — above all on womanhood and marriage, and on the questions she raised about missionary work — and by weighing everything under Scripture. She spent her life pointing away from herself to the God who had kept her, and this book tries to do the same.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
As for God, his way is perfect: the word of the LORD is tried: he is a buckler to all those that trust in him. PSALM 18:30

Most people who know the name Elisabeth Elliot know it because of one week in January 1956. Her husband Jim and four other young missionaries were killed by Waorani men on a sandbar of the Curaray River in the forest of eastern Ecuador, and she was left a widow at twenty-nine with a daughter of ten months. The story went round the world. It was told in magazines, preached from pulpits and retold in books for half a century, and it sent a generation of young people into missionary service. She told it first herself, in Through Gates of Splendor, published the following year.

But if that week were all, there would be no reason for a book like this one. What makes Elisabeth Elliot a teacher, and not only a figure in someone else’s story, is what she did with the rest of her life. She stayed in Ecuador. She went to live among the people who had killed her husband. She came home, wrote, married again, was widowed again, married a third time, and for some forty years taught, in books, at conferences, in a newsletter and on daily radio, a small number of things she had learned at great cost. She said them plainly and she said them often. Many thousands of Christians, a great many of them women, have counted her the person who taught them how to suffer, how to wait, how to obey, and how to trust God when He made no sense.

The one thread

If there is a single thread running through everything she taught, it is this: God is sovereign, and God is love, and both are true at the same time. Nothing reaches the believer that has not first passed through the hands of a Father who knows what He is doing and who will not waste it. Because that is so, the Christian can do three things that would otherwise be impossible. She can accept what God gives, including what she would never have chosen. She can obey Him in the next small duty without waiting to understand the whole. And she can offer everything — her losses as well as her gifts — back to Him, to be used as He pleases.

And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. ROMANS 8:28

Every chapter of this book is a variation on that theme. Her teaching on duty is that truth applied to the present hour. Her teaching on suffering is that truth applied to grief. Her teaching on obedience and discipline is that truth applied to the will, the body and the calendar. Her teaching on love and singleness is that truth applied to the heart’s strongest desire. Her teaching on the home is that truth applied to ordinary family life. And her teaching on mission is that truth applied to the work itself, which God does not need in order to be God, and which He may break when He chooses.

She did not arrive at this by speculation. She had been raised on it in a household that read the Bible at every meal, and then she had it tested beyond anything her upbringing could have imagined. What makes her worth hearing is not that she believed in the sovereignty of God, which many people do, but that she went on believing it when it had cost her almost everything, and that she was honest about how hard that was.

How this book is arranged

A chapter on her life comes first. Then fifteen short chapters set out her teaching. The first group lays the foundation: the God who is there, sovereign and loving; the old counsel to do the next thing; her conviction that suffering is never for nothing; and the movement from accepting what God gives to offering it back to Him. The second group follows that foundation into the shape of a Christian life: the liberty that is found in obedience, the disciplines of body, mind, time and feeling, love placed under the lordship of Christ, and loneliness. The third group takes up her teaching on womanhood, marriage and the home, the part of her work most often argued over. The fourth turns to mission and the cross: her honest questions about missionary work, and the way of dying to self that she learned from Amy Carmichael. The last group gathers her teaching on the inner life: the quiet heart, the questions we ask God, and thanksgiving in all things. A conclusion and a guide to her books close the volume.

Each chapter ends with points for reflection and action, and a prayer. She would have wanted that more than most. She had little patience with religion that stayed in the head, and she was fond of reminding her listeners that the point of knowing God’s will is to do it. Read a chapter at a time. Stop at the questions. Do one of the things they suggest before you go on.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

A word about her words

Elisabeth Elliot’s books remain in copyright, and many of them remain in print. This companion reproduces none of her words. Apart from the few-word watchwords by which she is remembered — to do the next thing, and that suffering is never for nothing — not a sentence of hers is quoted in these pages, not even the short sayings that circulate on cards and calendars. Every description of her teaching is a summary in our own language, and where her thought is set out it is set out as we understand it. Her books are named throughout so that the reader can go to the source, and the last chapter is a guide to them, with a suggestion of where to begin. Readers are warmly encouraged to buy them, borrow them and read them. Nothing here can replace the clarity and the dry, unsentimental warmth of her own voice.

The only words quoted are those of Scripture, in the Authorised Version on which she was raised; a few lines of an anonymous old poem, long in the public domain, from which she took her watchword; a line or two of old hymns of the kind her family sang; and one sentence of Amy Carmichael’s, from a book in the Ochorus library.

Where to read her with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and she would have been the first to object if it were. She had a sharp eye for hagiography, and in later life she took pains to correct the more glowing versions of her own story. Four cautions should be carried through these pages.

The first concerns her teaching on women and men. She held that God has ordered the sexes differently, that a wife is called to submit to her husband and that leadership in the church belongs to men, and she taught it without apology. Many Christians have been grateful for that teaching; others, equally committed to Scripture, have read the same passages differently and have found her tone at times more severe than the texts require. Chapter eleven sets out her view as fairly as we can and notes where believers part company.

The second concerns her manner. She could be brisk and stern. She had little sympathy for self-pity, and some readers, coming to her in fresh grief, have felt that she moved too quickly to acceptance and left too little room for lament. The Psalms make room for both, and we will try to do the same.

The third concerns her questions about mission. In No Graven Image and elsewhere she raised hard questions about missionary work — about what missionaries think they are achieving, and about a God who does not always bless the work done in His name. Some evangelical readers found this unsettling, and some still do. Chapter thirteen takes it up.

The fourth concerns her story. The events of 1956 have been told so often, and so gloriously, that the plain facts are easily lost. She herself grew more careful over the years in telling them, and later editions of her own first book acknowledged that what followed among the Waorani had not unfolded as simply as the early accounts implied. This book tries to keep to what is known.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Where she is faithful to the Word — and she is faithful far more often than not — receive her gladly. Where she presses beyond what is written, weigh it. She would not have wanted you to follow Elisabeth Elliot. She would have wanted you to follow Christ, and to do the next thing He gives you to do.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before reading further, write down the hardest thing God has allowed in your life so far. Keep the page, and return to it at the end of this book.

2. Ask yourself honestly whether you believe that God is both in control of your life and good. Tell Him plainly what you believe and what you do not.

3. If you know the story of 1956 only from sermons or films, note what you think you know. Hold it lightly as you read what follows.

4. Obtain one of her own books — Keep a Quiet Heart or Passion and Purity are good places to begin — and read it alongside these chapters.

5. Decide how you will read: one chapter a day or a week, with a Bible open and a few minutes of quiet after each prayer.

A PRAYER
Lord God, Your way is perfect, though I do not always understand it, and Your word has been tried in the fire and found true.
Thank You for the servants who have trusted You in the dark and told the rest of us what they found there.
As I read about one of them, keep me from admiring her and remaining unchanged. Turn my eyes from her courage to Your faithfulness.
Teach me to accept what You give, to obey You in the next thing, and to offer my whole life back to You, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Her Life
fields.body_html:
My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me. PSALM 31:15

A missionary household. Elisabeth Howard was born in Brussels on 21 December 1926, the second of six children of Philip E. Howard Jr. and Katharine Gillingham Howard, who were serving there as missionaries. The family returned to the United States while she was still a baby, and she grew up first in Germantown, in Philadelphia, and then in Moorestown, New Jersey. Her father became editor of the Sunday School Times, a widely read evangelical weekly. The household was ordered by Scripture: family worship morning and evening, hymns sung from memory, verses learned by heart, and a steady stream of missionaries passing through and sitting at the table. Summers were spent at the family’s place in Franconia, New Hampshire. Her brothers and sister — Philip, David, Virginia, Thomas and James — went in different directions; David became a leader in missions, and Thomas a writer who in later life became a Roman Catholic. Many years later she described that home, with gratitude and without pretending it was perfect, in The Shaping of a Christian Family.

School and Greek. For high school she was sent to Hampden DuBose Academy, a Christian boarding school in Florida. From 1944 to 1948 she studied at Wheaton College in Illinois, where she majored in Classical Greek. She meant to translate the Bible into an unwritten language, and she prepared for it with the same seriousness she brought to everything. At Wheaton she met a friend of her brother Dave, a wrestler and student of Greek from Portland, Oregon, named Jim Elliot.

Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. PROVERBS 3:5–6

The waiting years. What followed was one of the slowest courtships in the annals of evangelical romance, and one of the best known, because she later told it in Passion and Purity. The two were drawn to each other, and both were determined to put that attraction under the lordship of Christ. Jim was uncertain for a long time whether God was calling him to remain single for the sake of the work, and he would make no promise he was not sure he could keep. For some five years there was no engagement and very little certainty, much of the relationship carried on by letter across long distances. In those years she studied at Prairie Bible Institute in Three Hills, Alberta, and took linguistic training with the Summer Institute of Linguistics. Jim sailed for Ecuador with his friend Pete Fleming and arrived early in 1952. She went to Ecuador the same year, not as his fiancée but as a single missionary in her own right.

The Colorados. Her first assignment was among the Colorado people, now usually called the Tsáchila, at San Miguel de los Colorados in the western forest. With other single women missionaries she set out to reduce their unwritten language to writing. The work went slowly, and then went badly. Her chief language helper, a man named Don Macario, was murdered. Later a suitcase containing a great deal of her language work was stolen and never recovered. Months of labour were simply gone. She did not pretend to understand it, and many years afterwards she wrote about these losses, and what they had taught her about the God who does not explain Himself, in These Strange Ashes.

Quichua first. In January 1953 she and Jim were at last engaged, in Quito. He asked that she learn Quichua, the language of the people he was working among in the eastern jungle, before they married, and she did. That summer a flood swept away much of his station at Shandia. They were married in a civil ceremony in Quito on 8 October 1953, Jim’s twenty-sixth birthday, and went to live among the Quichua at Shandia and nearby. Their daughter, Valerie, was born on 27 February 1955.

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee. ISAIAH 43:2

The Curaray. For years the missionaries had heard of the Waorani — then known to outsiders by the slur “Auca” — a small people of the eastern forest feared for killing intruders. In the autumn of 1955 Jim, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully, Roger Youderian and the Mission Aviation Fellowship pilot Nate Saint began dropping gifts to a Waorani settlement from the air. On 3 January 1956 the five men landed on a sandbar of the Curaray River they called Palm Beach. Three days later they had a friendly meeting with a Waorani man and two women. On 8 January all five were speared to death. They had carried guns, and had agreed among themselves not to use them against the Waorani. A search party found their bodies some days later. Life magazine carried photographs, and the story of the five widows — Elisabeth, Marj Saint, Olive Fleming, Marilou McCully and Barbara Youderian — went round the world.

The widow at Shandia. She did not go home. She stayed at Shandia with her baby daughter and carried on the Quichua work her husband had left. In those first years she wrote Through Gates of Splendor, published in 1957, the account of the five men and their deaths that made the story known to millions, and Shadow of the Almighty, published in 1958, a life of Jim built round his journals. Both books sold in great numbers. Both would follow her for the rest of her life.

Among the Waorani. Meanwhile Dayuma, a Waorani woman who had fled her people years before, was teaching the language to Rachel Saint, Nate’s sister. In 1957 two Waorani women, Mintaka and Mankamu, came out of the forest, and lived for a time with Elisabeth, who began to learn their language from them. In October 1958 Elisabeth, with Valerie, then about three, and Rachel Saint, went with them and Dayuma to live among the Waorani. The people gave her the name Gikari, which means woodpecker. Over the following years several of those who had taken part in the killings came to faith in Christ, among them Kimo, Dyuwi and Mincaye, and in time Kimo and Dyuwi baptised Nate Saint’s children in the Curaray. Her relationship with Rachel Saint was strained, and in 1961 she left the Waorani and returned to Quichua work. The Savage My Kinsman, a book of photographs and text about those years, appeared in 1961.

Home. In 1963 she returned to the United States and settled in Franconia. She wrote. No Graven Image, a novel about a young missionary linguist, appeared in 1966; its ending, in which the missionary’s best efforts lead to a man’s death and no explanation is given, unsettled many evangelical readers who had expected a different sort of story from the widow of Jim Elliot. The Liberty of Obedience appeared in 1968, and the same year Who Shall Ascend, a life of the mission leader R. Kenneth Strachan.

For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. PSALM 30:5

Widowed again. On 1 January 1969 she married Addison H. Leitch, a professor of theology who taught at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary until his death. By her own account it was a happy marriage, and it was a short one. Leitch developed cancer, and she cared for him through his illness until he died in September 1973. She was forty-six, and a widow for the second time.

Lars, and Magnolia. In December 1977 she married Lars Gren, a former hospital chaplain who had boarded in her home. They made their home in Magnolia, Massachusetts, on the coast north of Boston, and he remained at her side for the rest of her life. Valerie married Walter Shepard, a Presbyterian minister, and they had eight children. Let Me Be a Woman, written as a series of letters for Valerie around the time of her marriage, had appeared in 1976.

The teaching years. The two decades that followed were the most fruitful of her life as a teacher. She taught as a writer and adjunct at Gordon-Conwell, spoke at conferences across the country and abroad, and from about 1982 to 2004 wrote The Elisabeth Elliot Newsletter, read by many thousands. The books came steadily: The Mark of a Man in 1981, Discipline: The Glad Surrender in 1982, Passion and Purity in 1984, A Chance to Die, her life of Amy Carmichael, in 1987, Loneliness in 1988, On Asking God Why in 1989, A Path Through Suffering in 1990, The Shaping of a Christian Family in 1992, Keep a Quiet Heart in 1995, Quest for Love in 1996, and others. From 1988 to 2001 her voice went out every weekday on the fifteen-minute radio programme Gateway to Joy, produced by Back to the Bible. Each broadcast began by reminding her listeners that they were loved with an everlasting love and that underneath were the everlasting arms.

The long twilight. From the early 2000s she suffered from a progressive dementia. Secure in the Everlasting Arms appeared in 2002 and Be Still My Soul in 2003, both gathered largely from earlier writing, and then she withdrew from public ministry. Lars cared for her at home in Magnolia through a long decline. She died there on 15 June 2015, aged eighty-eight.

Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come. PSALM 71:18

What kind of woman. Those who knew her describe a reserved, formidably disciplined woman with a measured voice, a dry wit and a strong dislike of fuss. She could be intimidating. She was not warm in the easy way, and she did not pretend to feelings she did not have. But she gave a great deal of time to people who wrote to her or sought her out, and she told the truth about her own struggles in a way that made strangers feel less alone. She would not have wanted her life remembered as a story of heroism. She would have wanted it remembered as a long obedience — a woman doing, for nearly ninety years, the next thing God gave her to do.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Her early language work was lost twice over, through a murder and a theft. Is there a labour of yours that seems to have come to nothing? Bring it to God by name.

2. She was widowed twice and did not stop serving. Think of one loss that has tempted you to withdraw from God’s work, and ask Him what faithfulness looks like now.

3. She went to live among the people who had killed her husband. Is there someone you have refused to go near because of what they did? Pray for them today.

4. Her home was ordered around Scripture, hymns and prayer. Choose one small habit of that kind and begin it in your own household this week.

5. Read Psalm 31 slowly, and put your own times — past, present and to come — into God’s hand.

A PRAYER
Father, my times are in Your hand: my birth and my schooling, my waiting and my losses, my work and my old age.
Thank You for the patience with which You led Your servant Elisabeth through the waters and the fire, and did not let them overflow her.
Where my work has come to nothing, teach me to trust You with it. Where I have been bereaved, keep me from shrinking back.
Make my life, too, a long obedience in the same direction, and carry me to the end, for the sake of Jesus Christ. Amen.

For high school she was sent to Hampden DuBose Academy, a Christian boarding school in Florida. From 1944 to 1948 she studied at Wheaton College in Illinois, where she majored in Classical Greek. She meant to translate the Bible into an unwritten language, and she prepared for it with the same seriousness she brought to everything. At Wheaton she met a friend of her brother Dave, a wrestler and student of Greek from Portland, Oregon, named Jim Elliot. Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. PROVERBS 3:5–6 The waiting years. What followed was one of the slowest courtships in the annals of evangelical romance, and one of the best known, because she later told it in Passion and Purity. The two were drawn to each other, and both were determined to put that attraction under the lordship of Christ. Jim was uncertain for a long time whether God was calling him to remain single for the sake of the work, and he would make no promise he was not sure he could keep. For some five years there was no engagement and very little certainty, much of the relationship carried on by letter across long distances. In those years she studied at Prairie Bible Institute in Three Hills, Alberta, and took linguistic training with the Summer Institute of Linguistics. Jim sailed for Ecuador with his friend Pete Fleming and arrived early in 1952. She went to Ecuador the same year, not as his fiancée but as a single missionary in her own right. The Colorados. Her first assignment was among the Colorado people, now usually called the Tsáchila, at San Miguel de los Colorados in the western forest. With other single women missionaries she set out to reduce their unwritten language to writing. The work went slowly, and then went badly. Her chief language helper, a man named Don Macario, was murdered. Later a suitcase containing a great deal of her language work was stolen and never recovered. Months of labour were simply gone. She did not pretend to understand it, and many years afterwards she wrote about these losses, and what they had taught her about the God who does not explain Himself, in These Strange Ashes. Quichua first. In January 1953 she and Jim were at last engaged, in Quito. He asked that she learn Quichua, the language of the people he was working among in the eastern jungle, before they married, and she did. That summer a flood swept away much of his station at Shandia. They were married in a civil ceremony in Quito on 8 October 1953, Jim’s twenty-sixth birthday, and went to live among the Quichua at Shandia and nearby. Their daughter, Valerie, was born on 27 February 1955. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee. In the autumn of 1955 Jim, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully, Roger Youderian and the Mission Aviation Fellowship pilot Nate Saint began dropping gifts to a Waorani settlement from the air. On 3 January 1956 the five men landed on a sandbar of the Curaray River they called Palm Beach. Three days later they had a friendly meeting with a Waorani man and two women. She did not go home. She stayed at Shandia with her baby daughter and carried on the Quichua work her husband had left. In those first years she wrote Through Gates of Splendor, published in 1957, the account of the five men and their deaths that made the story known to millions, and Shadow of the Almighty, published in 1958, a life of Jim built round his journals. Both books sold in great numbers. Both would follow her for the rest of her life. Among the Waorani. Meanwhile Dayuma, a Waorani woman who had fled her people years before, was teaching the language to Rachel Saint, Nate’s sister. No Graven Image, a novel about a young missionary linguist, appeared in 1966; its ending, in which the missionary’s best efforts lead to a man’s death and no explanation is given, unsettled many evangelical readers who had expected a different sort of story from the widow of Jim Elliot. The Liberty of Obedience appeared in 1968, and the same year Who Shall Ascend, a life of the mission leader R. Kenneth Strachan. For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. PSALM 30:5 Widowed again. On 1 January 1969 she married Addison H. Leitch, a professor of theology who taught at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary until his death. By her own account it was a happy marriage, and it was a short one. Leitch developed cancer, and she cared for him through his illness until he died in September 1973. She was forty-six, and a widow for the second time. Lars, and Magnolia. In December 1977 she married Lars Gren, a former hospital chaplain who had boarded in her home. They made their home in Magnolia, Massachusetts, on the coast north of Boston, and he remained at her side for the rest of her life. Valerie married Walter Shepard, a Presbyterian minister, and they had eight children. Let Me Be a Woman, written as a series of letters for Valerie around the time of her marriage, had appeared in 1976. The teaching years. The two decades that followed were the most fruitful of her life as a teacher. She taught as a writer and adjunct at Gordon-Conwell, spoke at conferences across the country and abroad, and from about 1982 to 2004 wrote The Elisabeth Elliot Newsletter, read by many thousands. From 1988 to 2001 her voice went out every weekday on the fifteen-minute radio programme Gateway to Joy, produced by Back to the Bible. Each broadcast began by reminding her listeners that they were loved with an everlasting love and that underneath were the everlasting arms. The long twilight. From the early 2000s she suffered from a progressive dementia. Secure in the Everlasting Arms appeared in 2002 and Be Still My Soul in 2003, both gathered largely from earlier writing, and then she withdrew from public ministry. Lars cared for her at home in Magnolia through a long decline. She died there on 15 June 2015, aged eighty-eight. Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come. PSALM 71:18 What kind of woman. Those who knew her describe a reserved, formidably disciplined woman with a measured voice, a dry wit and a strong dislike of fuss. She could be intimidating. She was not warm in the easy way, and she did not pretend to feelings she did not have. But she gave a great deal of time to people who wrote to her or sought her out, and she told the truth about her own struggles in a way that made strangers feel less alone. She would not have wanted her life remembered as a story of heroism. She would have wanted it remembered as a long obedience — a woman doing, for nearly ninety years, the next thing God gave her to do. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Her early language work was lost twice over, through a murder and a theft. Is there a labour of yours that seems to have come to nothing? Bring it to God by name. 2. She was widowed twice and did not stop serving. Think of one loss that has tempted you to withdraw from God’s work, and ask Him what faithfulness looks like now. 3. She went to live among the people who had killed her husband. Is there someone you have refused to go near because of what they did? Pray for them today. 4. Her home was ordered around Scripture, hymns and prayer. Choose one small habit of that kind and begin it in your own household this week. 5. Read Psalm 31 slowly, and put your own times — past, present and to come — into God’s hand. A PRAYER Father, my times are in Your hand: my birth and my schooling, my waiting and my losses, my work and my old age. Thank You for the patience with which You led Your servant Elisabeth through the waters and the fire, and did not let them overflow her. Where my work has come to nothing, teach me to trust You with it. Where I have been bereaved, keep me from shrinking back. Make my life, too, a long obedience in the same direction, and carry me to the end, for the sake of Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: The God Who Is There
fields.body_html:
The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them. DEUTERONOMY 33:27

For some thirteen years, every weekday, a great many people heard the same words at the start of a short radio programme. Before she said anything else on Gateway to Joy, Elisabeth Elliot reminded her listeners of two things: that the Lord had loved them with an everlasting love, and that underneath them were the everlasting arms. Both phrases come straight from the Authorised Version — the first from the prophet Jeremiah, the second from the last blessing of Moses. She did not begin with an illustration or a joke. She began with God.

The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee. JEREMIAH 31:3

That opening is the best possible summary of her theology. Everything else she taught — about duty, suffering, obedience, discipline, love and loneliness — stands on those two sentences. God loves you, and God holds you. His love is not a mood, and His arms are not a metaphor for good luck. They are the ground under the believer’s feet when every other ground has given way. The title of one of her later collections, Secure in the Everlasting Arms, puts the same conviction on its cover.

Sovereign and loving

She held the sovereignty of God without embarrassment. She believed, with a long line of Protestant teachers and with a great deal of plain Scripture, that God governs all things: the rise and fall of nations, the fall of a sparrow, a flood that sweeps away a mission station, and a spear on a sandbar in the Curaray. Nothing, in her teaching, happens to a child of God by accident. There is no corner of the universe where God is merely a spectator.

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? DANIEL 4:35

But she never taught sovereignty alone. A sovereign God who did not love would be a tyrant, and the doctrine would be a horror. What made it a comfort to her was that the One who rules all things is the same One who did not spare His own Son. The question of whether God can be trusted with what He permits had, for her, already been answered at Calvary. If He gave His Son for us, He will not be careless with anything else.

He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? ROMANS 8:32

This is the hinge of her whole outlook. Many people believe that God is powerful and doubt that He is kind. Many others believe that He is kind and doubt that He is in charge. She insisted on both, and she insisted on them most firmly at the moments when they seemed most impossible to hold together.

Not fatalism

It is important to see what this teaching is not. It is not fatalism, the shrug that says whatever will be will be. The fatalist submits to an impersonal force; the Christian trusts a Person. The fatalist concludes that nothing he does matters; Elisabeth Elliot concluded that everything he does matters, because God has given him real duties and will hold him to them. She never used the sovereignty of God as an excuse for laziness or carelessness, and she had sharp words for those who did.

Nor is it a claim to understand. She was quite clear that God’s purposes are mostly hidden from us. She did not know why Macario was murdered, or why her language files were stolen, or why five young men who had prepared so carefully were killed within days of their first friendly meeting. She did not offer neat explanations, and she distrusted those who did. Her confidence was not in her ability to read God’s purposes but in His character. She knew who He was, even when she did not know what He was doing.

For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts. ISAIAH 55:8–9

This combination — great confidence about God and great reticence about His reasons — is one of the most valuable things she offers. It saves the sufferer from two opposite errors: the despair that concludes God has lost control, and the glib comfort that pretends to know exactly why He has done what He has done.

The God who speaks

Behind all of this lay her conviction that God has made Himself known in the Bible, and that the Bible is to be believed and obeyed. She had been trained in Greek and could read the New Testament in its own language, and she was also a woman who read the Bible daily, memorised a great deal of it, and quoted it constantly. She did not treat Scripture as a collection of helpful thoughts. She treated it as the voice of the God who is there, speaking to people who would otherwise be left guessing.

That is why her teaching keeps returning to the text. When she was asked how to know God’s will, she pointed first to what He has already said. When she was asked how to bear a loss, she pointed to the Psalms and to the cross. When she was asked about feelings, she pointed to promises that do not depend on feelings. The God who is there is also the God who has spoken, and for her the two could not be separated.

Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105

Weighing it

Her doctrine of God is, in its main lines, the doctrine of historic Protestant Christianity, and evangelical readers can receive it with gratitude. Three cautions are worth adding.

The first is that the sovereignty of God can be taught in a way that leaves no room for lament. Scripture does not do this. The same Psalms that declare God’s rule also cry out against Him, ask how long, and complain that He has hidden His face. She knew the Psalms as well as anyone, and she did not forbid honest crying; but readers who find her counsel brisk should remember that the Bible gives them words for protest as well as for surrender.

The second is that the language of God’s sovereignty can be misused by the strong against the weak — as when someone in authority tells a victim to accept, as God’s will, a wrong that ought to be resisted. She never meant her teaching that way, and she spoke plainly against sin; but the distinction matters. To accept what God permits is not to approve what men do.

The third is simply that this is a doctrine to be lived before it is argued. She did not come to it as a debater. She came to it as a widow on a mission station with a baby, and she held it because, when everything else had gone, it held her.

It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. LAMENTATIONS 3:22–23
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Which do you find harder to believe — that God is in control, or that God is good? Tell Him honestly, and ask Him to strengthen what is weak.

2. Read Romans 8:28–39 slowly. Underline every phrase that speaks of God’s love and every phrase that speaks of His power.

3. Think of a present trouble whose purpose you cannot see. Write down what you know of God’s character, and set it beside what you do not know of His reasons.

4. Learn Deuteronomy 33:27 and Jeremiah 31:3 by heart, and say them to yourself each morning this week before you say anything else.

5. Consider whether you have ever used the will of God as an excuse for doing nothing. Name one duty you have been avoiding, and do it.

A PRAYER
Eternal God, You are my refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms. You have loved me with an everlasting love.
You rule all things, and none can stay Your hand; and You did not spare Your own Son for me. Teach me to hold both truths together.
When I cannot see what You are doing, let me rest in who You are. When I am tempted to despair, remind me that Your mercies are new every morning.
Hold me when I cannot hold on, and keep me trusting You to the end, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Do the Next Thing
fields.body_html:
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest. ECCLESIASTES 9:10

If Elisabeth Elliot had a motto, it was four words long. She did not invent it. She found it in an anonymous old poem, written in imitation of antique English spelling, which tells of a message carried from an old parsonage by the sea, said to have been carved there as an ancient inscription. The refrain of the poem is a single counsel: “Doe the nexte thynge.” She quoted it for decades, in her writing, in her talks and on the radio, and it became so closely tied to her name that many people assume she wrote it. She did not, and she never claimed to. But she made it her own.

The poem and the counsel

The poem is a simple piece of old devotional verse, and its argument is simple too. The believer who is anxious about the future, bewildered by guidance, or overwhelmed by the size of what lies ahead is not asked to see the whole road. He is asked to take the next step, trusting God with the rest. The poem puts it in a couplet that captures her teaching almost exactly: “Moment by moment, let down from Heaven, / Time, opportunity, and guidance are given.”

That is the heart of it. God does not give us tomorrow’s strength today, or next year’s guidance this morning. He gives what is needed for the present hour, and He asks for obedience in the present hour. The rest He keeps in His own hands.

Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. MATTHEW 6:34

She made it plain that this counsel had carried her through the darkest seasons of her life. When the news came from the Curaray, there was still a baby to feed, a station to run, and Quichua believers who needed teaching. When Addison Leitch was dying, there was still the daily care of a sick man. She did not find the strength for widowhood in a single heroic act of resignation. She found it in the next duty, and then the next, and then the next.

Duty is not a dirty word

In an age that prizes self-expression, she spoke unashamedly of duty. She believed that most of God’s will for most people, most of the time, is not hidden at all. It is the plain task in front of them: the dishes, the letter, the child, the job, the neighbour, the prayer. The Christian who is waiting for a great sign before doing anything has usually overlooked a great deal of guidance already given.

And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. COLOSSIANS 3:23

This was not drudgery dressed up as piety. She held that ordinary work, done for God, is a form of worship, and that there is a peculiar freedom in it. The person who does the next thing is released from the tyranny of the whole. She does not have to solve her life. She has only to be faithful in the hour she has been given. Jesus pointed His disciples to the same freedom when He told them that the one who is faithful in the least is faithful also in much.

Closely tied to this was her conviction that the present moment is the only place where we can meet God. The past is forgiven and finished; the future is not yet given. Anxiety, as she often observed, lives almost entirely in the future, in imagined disasters that may never come and for which no grace has yet been supplied. Regret lives in the past. But God is the God of today, and today is where He gives His help.

This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. PSALM 118:24

Many of the short pieces gathered from her newsletter in Keep a Quiet Heart return to this theme in one form or another, for readers lying awake with worry, stuck at a decision, or unable to imagine the years ahead. Again and again her counsel is the same. Do not try to carry tomorrow. Ask what God has given you to do now, and do it. The quiet heart, in her teaching, is not a heart that has understood everything. It is a heart that has stopped trying to carry what belongs to God.

Obedience as the way to light

There is a further point here, and it is easy to miss. She believed that obedience is often the way to understanding, and not the other way round. We want to see before we act. God frequently asks us to act before we see. The next step taken in faith becomes the place from which the step after it can be seen. Guidance, in her teaching, is less like a map handed over at the start of a journey and more like a lamp carried along a dark path, lighting a few yards at a time.

If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself. JOHN 7:17

This is why she had so little patience with endless introspection about God’s will. She did not despise the question; she had agonised over it herself, through years of uncertainty about marriage and missionary service. But she came to believe that most people who say they do not know God’s will are not lacking information. They are lacking obedience to what they already know. Do that, she would say in substance, and more light will come.

Who is among you that feareth the LORD, that obeyeth the voice of his servant, that walketh in darkness, and hath no light? let him trust in the name of the LORD, and stay upon his God. ISAIAH 50:10

Weighing it

This is one of the most practically useful things she ever taught, and it rests on solid ground. Jesus Himself forbade anxiety about tomorrow, and the wisdom literature everywhere commends diligence in the task at hand. Two cautions are worth adding.

The first is that the next thing is not always the obvious thing. Sometimes the next thing God gives is to stop, to rest, to grieve, to seek counsel, or to change direction altogether. A rule of duty, applied mechanically, can become a way of running from what God is saying. She would have agreed; the next thing, for her, was always the next thing God gave, not merely the next item on a list.

The second is that busyness can masquerade as obedience. A person can keep doing the next thing in order to avoid ever asking the larger question. The cure is not to abandon the counsel but to remember its root. It is not a technique for getting through the day. It is an act of trust in the God who holds the whole day, and the whole life, in His hand.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. What is the next thing God has given you to do today? Write it down, and do it before you read further.

2. Name one anxiety about the future that you have been carrying. Ask whether any grace has yet been given for it, and hand it back to God.

3. Think of a decision on which you have been waiting for clearer guidance. Is there something you already know you should do? Do that first.

4. Choose one ordinary task this week — washing up, a commute, a routine report — and do it deliberately as an offering to the Lord.

She did not, and she never claimed to. But she made it her own. The poem and the counsel The poem is a simple piece of old devotional verse, and its argument is simple too. fields.title: Suffering Is Never for Nothing
fields.body_html:
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:17

Elisabeth Elliot did not choose suffering as her subject. It chose her. By the time she was forty-six she had lost her chief language helper to murder, her language work to theft, her first husband to Waorani spears and her second to cancer. She had lived in the forest among the men who killed Jim, and she had been misunderstood by fellow missionaries and by many readers at home. When she spoke about suffering, people listened, because they knew she was not speaking from a study. And the thing she said most often, in five words that became a watchword, was that suffering is never for nothing.

What suffering is

She defined suffering very broadly. It was not only the dramatic losses — death, illness, betrayal — but every kind of disappointment and every kind of lack, large or small. The woman who longs for a husband and has none, the man who has a job he hates and cannot leave, the parents of a child who has gone astray, the elderly person who has outlived every friend: all of these, in her teaching, are suffering, and all of them are matters with which God is concerned. She took the small sorrows seriously as well as the great ones, and she had no patience with a ranking that told people their pain did not count because someone else had worse.

That broad definition had a practical purpose. If suffering is as wide as that, then everyone is suffering in some way, and everyone needs to know what to do with it. Her teaching on the subject was not a special consolation for the bereaved. It was a basic part of the Christian life.

The seed and the harvest

In A Path Through Suffering, published in 1990, she worked out her teaching through images from the natural world. The book draws on the little parables of Lilias Trotter, the Victorian artist who gave her life to mission in Algeria, who had found in seeds, leaves and flowers pictures of the way life comes through letting go and dying. Behind them all stands the Lord’s own saying about the grain of wheat.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. JOHN 12:24

Her point was that in God’s world death is the way to life, and loss the way to fruitfulness. This is not because suffering is good in itself. It is because God, who raised Christ from the dead, is in the business of bringing life out of death. The seed does not enjoy the darkness of the soil, and Scripture never asks it to pretend it does. But the soil is not the end of the seed’s story.

Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit. JOHN 15:2

Underneath this, and more important than any illustration from nature, was the cross. She believed that the Christian’s suffering can only be understood in the light of Christ’s. He did not avoid suffering; He walked straight into it, for the joy that was set before Him. And the cross, the worst thing that has ever happened, the murder of the Son of God, became the means of the world’s salvation. If God could do that with Calvary, her teaching runs, He can do something with our smaller crosses.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

She also pressed the apostolic teaching that believers share in Christ’s sufferings. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned us; it is part of what it means to belong to a crucified Lord. Paul wanted to know Christ not only in the power of His resurrection but in the fellowship of His sufferings, and she believed that this fellowship was a privilege, though rarely one we would choose.

That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death. PHILIPPIANS 3:10

Never for nothing

What did she mean by saying that suffering is never for nothing? She did not mean that every suffering has a purpose we can identify. She was clear that we usually cannot. She meant that God wastes nothing. No pain endured by one of His children is meaningless in His hands. It may teach patience; it may humble pride; it may prepare us to comfort others; it may simply be the place where we learn that He is enough. And beyond all that it is preparing something eternal, a weight of glory that will make the present affliction look light.

For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. ROMANS 8:18

She was also clear that suffering is not automatically sanctifying. Pain can make people bitter as easily as it makes them holy. What makes the difference is what we do with it — whether we resent it, or receive it from God’s hand and offer it back to Him. That movement, from acceptance to offering, is the subject of the next chapter, and in her teaching it was the key to everything.

Weighing it

Her teaching on suffering is deeply biblical, and it has helped a very great number of people. It is also demanding, and two cautions should be carried with it.

The first is that she wrote from a position of great personal strength and a temperament not much given to display. Some readers, especially those in raw grief, have felt that she moved too quickly to the lesson and too slowly through the tears. Scripture allows a long time for weeping. Job sat in the ashes for many chapters before God spoke, and the Lord Himself wept at a graveside where He was about to raise the dead. The promise that suffering is never for nothing is true, but it is not always the first thing a grieving person needs to hear.

The second is that the language of fruitfulness can be misheard as a promise of visible results. Some suffering bears no fruit that anyone on earth will ever see. The grain of wheat dies in the dark, and the harvest may be gathered long after the sower is gone. She knew this; her own first language work came to nothing. The comfort is not that we will see the reason, but that God will not waste the loss.

Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. HEBREWS 12:11
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Taking suffering as broadly as she did, where are you suffering now — in a great loss or in a small, daily disappointment? Name it plainly before God.

2. Read John 12:20–33. Consider what in your own life may need to fall into the ground and die.

3. Think of someone who comforted you in a past trouble out of their own experience of pain. Thank God for them, and if you can, thank them.

4. Is there a suffering of yours that has made you bitter rather than gentle? Confess it, and ask God to begin to change its fruit.

5. Obtain A Path Through Suffering, or one of Lilias Trotter’s own little books of parables, and read one meditation each day this week.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You endured the cross for the joy set before You, and You know every sorrow I carry.
I do not understand why You have allowed what You have allowed. But I believe that You waste nothing, and that my suffering is not for nothing in Your hands.
Keep me from bitterness. Let what has broken me make me more like You, and give me words to comfort others with the comfort You have given me.
Bring out of my small deaths the life that only You can give, and at the last the glory You have promised. Amen.

fields.title: Acceptance and Offering
fields.body_html:
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

If suffering is never for nothing, what is the believer to do with it? Elisabeth Elliot’s answer had two movements, and she returned to them so often that they form the practical core of her teaching. The first is acceptance: receiving what God has given, including what we would never have chosen, as from His hand. The second is offering: giving it back to Him as a sacrifice, to be used as He pleases. Between them, she believed, lies the transformation of suffering. What is merely endured remains a loss. What is accepted and offered becomes a gift.

Receiving from His hand

Acceptance, in her teaching, did not mean pretending. It did not mean saying that a loss did not hurt, or that it was good in itself, or that we ought to feel happy about it. It meant something both simpler and harder: acknowledging that this, too, has come through the hands of a loving and sovereign God, and refusing to fight Him over it.

And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. JOB 1:21

Job’s words were among her touchstones. He did not say that Satan had taken away, or the Sabeans, or the wind. He said the Lord had taken away, and he blessed Him. That is not resignation to fate; it is worship in the dark. And Job’s next response, to his wife, put the matter even more sharply.

But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips. JOB 2:10

She often noted, in substance, that we are glad to accept God’s sovereignty when it brings us what we want. The test of faith is whether we accept it when it does not. Acceptance is the refusal to divide our lives into the parts God has arranged and the parts that have escaped Him.

Amy Carmichael, whose life Elisabeth Elliot wrote in A Chance to Die, gave this a phrase in the title of one of her poems: “In Acceptance Lieth Peace.” It names exactly what Elisabeth Elliot found. Peace does not come when the circumstances change. It comes when the will stops fighting the God who allowed them.

Offering it back

But acceptance alone could become passive, even stoical. What made her teaching distinctively Christian was the second movement. Having received what God gave, the believer is to offer it back to Him. The widowhood, the singleness, the illness, the disappointment, the loneliness — all of it is to be laid on the altar as a living sacrifice.

The feeding of the five thousand gives a picture of it in the boy with his lunch. He had five barley loaves and two small fishes, absurdly little for such a crowd. The disciples could see only the inadequacy. But when the little was given to Jesus, He blessed it, broke it, and fed thousands with it.

There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many? JOHN 6:9

Her point was that our losses, like the boy’s lunch, are worth nothing much in our own hands. In Christ’s hands they become bread for others. A woman who has accepted her singleness and offered it to God may find it becomes a means of service no married woman could give. A widow who has offered her grief may find it becomes the ground of comfort for a hundred other widows. That, in her teaching, is the transformation of suffering: not that the loss stops being a loss, but that it becomes an offering, and God accepts offerings and uses them.

She was clear that a real offering costs something. David refused to offer the Lord what had cost him nothing, and she believed the same principle applied to the sacrifices of the heart. It is easy to offer God what we do not want. The offering that transforms is the offering of what we did want — the hope, the person, the plan — given up because He asked.

And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. 2 SAMUEL 24:24

This is why her teaching on acceptance was never cheap. She was not asking people to make the best of things. She was asking them to make a sacrifice of things, and to trust God with the result. The model, as always for her, was Christ in Gethsemane, who asked that the cup might pass from Him and then took it from His Father’s hand.

And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. MATTHEW 26:39

Loneliness and widowhood

She applied this teaching most directly to the losses she knew best. She was widowed twice, and she lived long seasons alone. She did not romanticise either. But she taught that loneliness, like any other suffering, can be accepted and offered, and that when it is, God meets the lonely person in it. Her book Loneliness, written after both her widowhoods, works this out at length, and chapter ten of this companion looks at it more closely.

What she wanted the bereaved and the lonely to know was that their state, however painful, was not a waste of their lives. It was material for an offering. The question was not whether they would suffer — they already were — but what they would do with it. They could clutch it and resent it, or they could open their hands and give it to God. The first leaves us alone with our loss. The second, she believed, brings us into fellowship with Him.

Weighing it

This is, perhaps, the most characteristic thing she taught, and it is thoroughly scriptural. Paul calls the whole of the believer’s life a living sacrifice; the writer to the Hebrews speaks of the sacrifice of praise; and the Lord Himself prayed, not my will but Thine. Two cautions are worth noting.

The first is that acceptance of what God permits is not the same as acceptance of injustice that ought to be resisted. A Christian may accept from God’s hand an illness that cannot be cured; she is not thereby required to accept abuse that can be stopped. Elisabeth Elliot’s teaching concerned the things God sends that we cannot change, and it should not be stretched to cover the things we can and should change.

The second is that acceptance is usually not a single act. Most people who lose something precious have to give it back to God again and again, sometimes every morning. That is not failure. It is the shape of the offering in a fallen world, and God is patient with those who must lay the same sacrifice on the altar many times.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. PSALM 51:17
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name one thing in your life that you have not yet accepted from God’s hand. Tell Him honestly why you are fighting it.

2. Read Job 1 and 2. Notice where Job locates the source of his losses, and how he responds.

3. Take the loss or limitation you named, and in a deliberate prayer offer it to God as a living sacrifice. Write down the date.

4. Think of someone who is lonely or bereaved. Ask how your own experience of loss, offered to God, might become bread for them this week.

5. If you have offered something to God before and taken it back, offer it again today without shame.

A PRAYER
Father, You gave and You have taken away. Blessed be Your name.
I confess that I have received Your good gifts gladly and fought You over the hard ones. Teach me to receive everything from Your hand.
Here is what I have lost and what I lack. It is small in my hands. I give it to You as a living sacrifice; bless it, break it, and use it as You will.
Not my will but Yours be done, as it was in Gethsemane, for the sake of Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

What she wanted the bereaved and the lonely to know was that their state, however painful, was not a waste of their lives. It was material for an offering. The question was not whether they would suffer — they already were — but what they would do with it. They could clutch it and resent it, or they could open their hands and give it to God. The first leaves us alone with our loss. The second, she believed, brings us into fellowship with Him. Paul calls the whole of the believer’s life a living sacrifice; the writer to the Hebrews speaks of the sacrifice of praise; and the Lord Himself prayed, not my will but Thine. A Christian may accept from God’s hand an illness that cannot be cured; she is not thereby required to accept abuse that can be stopped. The second is that acceptance is usually not a single act. Most people who lose something precious have to give it back to God again and again, sometimes every morning. That is not failure. It is the shape of the offering in a fallen world, and God is patient with those who must lay the same sacrifice on the altar many times. Notice where Job locates the source of his losses, and how he responds. 3. Take the loss or limitation you named, and in a deliberate prayer offer it to God as a living sacrifice. Write down the date. 4. Think of someone who is lonely or bereaved. Ask how your own experience of loss, offered to God, might become bread for them this week. 5. I confess that I have received Your good gifts gladly and fought You over the hard ones. Teach me to receive everything from Your hand. Here is what I have lost and what I lack. It is small in my hands. I give it to You as a living sacrifice; bless it, break it, and use it as You will. Not my will but Yours be done, as it was in Gethsemane, for the sake of Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.body_html:
And I will walk at liberty: for I seek thy precepts. PSALM 119:45

Most people assume that freedom and obedience are opposites. To be free is to do as we please; to obey is to give that freedom up. Elisabeth Elliot spent much of her teaching life arguing that this assumption is exactly backwards. The title of one of her earliest books of teaching, The Liberty of Obedience, published in 1968, states the paradox in four words. True liberty, she believed, is found only in obedience to God, and the person who refuses to obey is not free at all but enslaved to his own will, his own appetites and the opinions of others.

A book written after the forest

The Liberty of Obedience is a short book, drawn in part, it appears, from articles she had written for the Sunday School Times, and it came out of a particular moment in her life. She had returned from Ecuador a few years before, after years among Quichua and Waorani people whose ways of life were utterly unlike those of the American evangelicalism she had grown up in. Living among them had shown her how much of what she had been taught to call Christian was really cultural — habits of dress, manners and recreation that had little to do with the commands of God and a great deal to do with the customs of a particular kind of American church. At the same time it had shown her, more sharply than ever, the commands of God that do not change from one culture to another.

The book is in large part an attempt to distinguish the two. On one side she set the rules invented by men, which may be useful but which bind no conscience. On the other she set the commands of God, which bind every conscience everywhere. Much of the trouble in the churches, she suggested, comes from confusing them: holding people to man-made rules as though they were divine, and treating divine commands as though they were optional.

But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. MATTHEW 15:9

Against legalism

On the first point she was a sharp critic of legalism. She had seen missionaries try to impose on new believers the customs of their home churches, and she had seen at home how easily a list of forbidden activities could stand in for holiness. She believed that a Christian who measures godliness by what he avoids has missed the heart of the matter. The kingdom of God is not food and drink, Paul said, but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Ghost.

For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. ROMANS 14:17

This put her somewhat at odds with parts of the world she came from. But her book was not a call to loosen up. It was a call to take God’s commands more seriously, not less, by refusing to let man-made rules crowd them out.

Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. GALATIANS 5:1

On the second point she was just as firm. If legalism is the error of adding to God’s commands, licence is the error of subtracting from them. The book appeared at a time when many in the wider culture, and some in the churches, were arguing that love alone was the only rule, and that any fixed moral command was a kind of bondage. She disagreed. Christian liberty, she insisted, is not freedom from God’s law but freedom for it — the freedom of a creature who has been released from sin in order to do what she was made to do.

For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. GALATIANS 5:13

One way to put her point is to picture a creature fulfilling its design. A train is not freer when it leaves the rails. A fish is not freer when it leaves the water. A human being, made in the image of God and for fellowship with Him, is most free when she is doing His will, and least free when she is doing her own. Disobedience feels like freedom for a moment, and then it binds.

Obedience as love

What kept her teaching on obedience from becoming grim was her conviction that obedience is the language of love. Jesus Himself made the connection: if you love Me, keep My commandments. She did not see the commands of God as arbitrary hurdles set up to test us, but as the expressed wishes of One who loves us and knows what is good for us. To obey them is to trust Him.

If ye love me, keep my commandments. JOHN 14:15

She also held, as we saw in chapter four, that obedience is the way to knowledge. The person who waits to understand before obeying will wait for ever. The person who obeys what she already knows will be given more light. This was not an abstract principle for her. She had obeyed, step by step, through years when she understood very little of what God was doing, and she believed that the understanding had come, when it came, through the obedience.

Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. JOHN 8:31–32

Weighing it

Her teaching here stands squarely in the line of Paul’s letters to the Galatians and the Romans, and of the Lord’s own words in John’s Gospel. The distinction between the commands of God and the traditions of men is one every generation needs to relearn. Two cautions are worth carrying.

The first is that the line between God’s commands and men’s rules is not always easy to draw, and sincere Christians draw it in different places. What one believer regards as a cultural habit another regards as a matter of conscience. Paul’s counsel in Romans 14 — that each should be fully persuaded in his own mind, and should not despise or judge the other — is the necessary companion to her teaching. She would not have disagreed, though she was more confident than most about where the line fell.

The second is that the language of obedience can be used to cover a merely external conformity. She meant something deeper: the obedience of a heart that loves God and wants His will. A person who keeps every command out of fear, without love, has not found the liberty she was describing. He has found another kind of bondage.

But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed. JAMES 1:25
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where in your life does freedom feel like the opposite of obedience? Ask God to show you whether your idea of freedom is His.

2. Make two short lists: rules you keep that come from your church culture, and commands you keep that come plainly from Scripture. Notice which list is longer.

3. Is there a man-made rule by which you have been judging another Christian? Confess it, and read Romans 14.

4. Is there a plain command of God that you have been treating as optional? Name it, and take one step of obedience today.

5. Read Galatians 5 slowly, noting every mention of liberty and every mention of the flesh.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have called me to liberty, and I have often mistaken my own will for freedom.
Deliver me from the bondage of rules You never gave, and from the bondage of desires You never blessed.
Teach me that Your commandments are not grievous, and that to obey You is to walk at liberty.
Let my obedience be the obedience of love, and lead me into the freedom of the children of God, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.
