fields.title: Discipline: The Glad Surrender
fields.body_html:
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. 1 CORINTHIANS 6:19–20

Discipline is not a fashionable word, and Elisabeth Elliot knew it. She used it anyway, and she gave it a subtitle that changed its colour: The Glad Surrender. Her book of that name, published in 1982, sets out what she believed the disciplined Christian life looks like in practice. It is one of the most concrete things she wrote, and one of the most searching. It is also, for all its demands, a book about joy, because she believed that discipline rightly understood is not the grim effort of a person trying to improve himself, but the glad response of a person who has been called by God and wants to answer.

Called, then disciplined

The order of the book matters. Before it says anything about how a Christian should manage the body, the mind or the clock, it sets out who the Christian is. We are created by God, cared for by Him and called by Him. Discipline is the answer to that call. It is not the way we earn God’s favour; it is the way we respond to it. The book speaks of the Christian as under orders, and the picture fits: a soldier does not obey in order to become a soldier. He obeys because he already is one.

Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. ISAIAH 6:8

This saves her teaching from moralism. The disciplines she describes are not techniques for self-improvement. They are acts of surrender to a Master. And because the Master is good, the surrender can be glad.

The body and the mind

She began, characteristically, with the body. She had no time for a piety that despised the body or ignored it. The body is God’s gift and the Spirit’s temple, and it is to be cared for, kept in order and brought under control. She wrote plainly about eating, sleeping, exercise and the ordinary self-indulgences that slowly master us. The apostle kept his body under, lest he should be a castaway; and Christians who cannot say no to their appetites will find it hard to say yes to God.

But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:27

From the body she moved to the mind. She believed that what we allow into our minds shapes what we become, and that the Christian is responsible for her thoughts as well as her deeds. That meant choosing what to read, what to watch and what to dwell on, and it meant taking every thought captive to Christ rather than letting the mind wander wherever it liked.

Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ. 2 CORINTHIANS 10:5

She went on to four disciplines that are less often discussed. The discipline of place is the acceptance of where God has put us — the town, the house, the station in life — rather than a restless longing to be somewhere else. She had lived in a jungle clearing, a Waorani settlement, a New England village and a house by the sea, and she believed that contentment is learned, as Paul said he had learned it, in whatever state we find ourselves.

Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. PHILIPPIANS 4:11

The discipline of time is the stewardship of the hours God gives. She was famously orderly in her own use of time, and she believed that most people who say they have no time for prayer or Scripture have plenty of time for other things. The discipline of possessions is the refusal to let things own us, and the willingness to give, to do without, and to hold everything loosely. The discipline of work is the doing of whatever we are given to do, paid or unpaid, as service to God — the same conviction that lay behind her watchword, do the next thing.

So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. PSALM 90:12

The discipline of feelings

The last discipline she discussed is in some ways the hardest, and the most characteristic of her teaching. She believed that feelings, though real and God-given, are not to rule us. We cannot always choose what we feel, but we can choose what we do with what we feel. We can refuse to let a mood dictate our actions, decline to nurse a resentment, and act in love towards someone when we do not feel loving. Over time, she believed, the feelings often follow the obedience. But even when they do not, the obedience stands.

This was, for her, not repression but order. The heart is to be kept, as Proverbs says, with all diligence, because out of it are the issues of life. A Christian who is governed by her feelings is at the mercy of every change in her health, her sleep and her circumstances. A Christian who has brought her feelings under the lordship of Christ is free to love, serve and obey whatever the weather inside.

Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. PROVERBS 4:23

The book ends where it began, with the call. The whole of the disciplined life, in her teaching, is simply the giving of one’s life to the One who gave His for us. Frances Ridley Havergal put the same surrender into a hymn that generations of Christians have sung: “Take my will, and make it Thine; / It shall be no longer mine.”

Weighing it

Her teaching on discipline is thoroughly biblical in substance, and it is a needed corrective in an age that often treats self-control as unhealthy and self-expression as a virtue. Two cautions are worth adding.

The first concerns temperament. She was by nature orderly, energetic and self-controlled, and some of her readers are not. A person who struggles with chronic illness, depression or a chaotic household may read her and feel only condemnation. That was not her intention, and Scripture does not lay the same burdens on every back. The disciplines are meant to be received as an invitation into freedom, not as a standard to beat oneself with.

The second concerns the feelings. Her teaching that feelings must not rule us is right, but it can be heard as teaching that feelings do not matter. They do. The Psalms are full of them, and the Lord Himself was troubled, grieved and moved with compassion. The aim of the discipline of feelings is not to silence them but to bring them, honestly expressed, under the rule of Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Of the disciplines she names — body, mind, place, time, possessions, work and feelings — which do you find hardest? Choose one to work on this month.

2. Read 1 Corinthians 9:24–27, and ask what in your daily habits is mastering you rather than being mastered.

3. Keep a simple record of how you spend your time for three days. Compare it with what you say your priorities are.

4. Give away one possession this week that you would rather keep, as an act of loosening your grip.

5. Next time you are ruled by a feeling, stop, name it honestly before God, and then do the next right thing regardless.

A PRAYER
Lord, You created me, You care for me, and You have called me. I am not my own; I have been bought with a price.
I give You my body, my mind, my place, my time, my possessions, my work and my feelings. Take them, and bring them into order under Your hand.
Where I have been mastered by my appetites or my moods, set me free. Where I have been careless with what You have given, forgive me.
Make my surrender glad and not grudging, and let my whole life glorify You, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Passion and Purity
fields.body_html:
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please. SONG OF SOLOMON 2:7

Of all Elisabeth Elliot’s books, the one most often pressed into the hands of young Christians is Passion and Purity, published in 1984. It is part memoir and part counsel. Its subtitle speaks of learning to bring one’s love life under Christ’s control, and it does so by telling the story of her own long, uncertain and restrained courtship with Jim Elliot. For many thousands of young people it has been the first book to take seriously both the strength of their desires and the claim of Christ upon them.

The story she told

She told it frankly. She described meeting Jim at Wheaton, the growing attraction between them, and the years of uncertainty that followed. He was unsure whether God was calling him to remain single, and he would not commit himself to her until he was sure. She, for her part, would not pursue him. They wrote letters, often long ones, across great distances; they saw each other seldom; and for about five years they did not know whether they would ever marry. She drew on her journals and on their correspondence to show what that waiting felt like from the inside — the hope, the frustration, the temptation to take matters into their own hands, and the repeated laying of the whole thing on the altar.

It is important to say that she did not hold up their story as a pattern to be copied exactly. Few couples will wait as long, and few should. What she held up was the principle beneath it: that love, like every other part of life, belongs to God, and is to be placed under His lordship rather than left to rule us.

Love under lordship

The heart of the book is that conviction. Romantic love is a gift of God and one of the strongest forces in human life. It is not to be despised, and she did not despise it; her own love for Jim was intense, and she did not hide it. But precisely because it is so strong, it is dangerous when it is not under Christ’s control. It can become an idol. It can override conscience, judgement and obedience. It can lead people into marriages God never meant, or into intimacies that belong only to marriage.

Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. PSALM 37:4

Her counsel was that the believer should put the whole matter into God’s hands — the attraction, the hope, the person — and leave it there. This is the same movement of acceptance and offering we have already seen, applied to the heart’s strongest desire. The young woman who loves a man is to offer that love to God, as Abraham offered Isaac, not knowing whether it will be given back. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is not. In either case, she believed, the offering is not wasted.

Purity

The second half of the title is purity, and she was unambiguous about it. Sexual intimacy belongs within marriage and nowhere else. She did not apologise for that teaching, and she did not soften it. But she grounded it not in fear or prudishness but in the holiness of God and the goodness of His design. The body is the Lord’s, and to keep it pure is to honour Him with it.

For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:3–4

She also pressed for purity of heart and imagination, not only of conduct. She knew how much of the battle is fought in the mind, and she urged young people to guard what they allowed themselves to dwell on, to avoid situations that made temptation easy, and to keep their emotional commitments within the bounds of what had actually been promised. A heart given away too soon, she believed, can be as damaging as a body given away too soon.

Running through the whole book is the theme of waiting. She believed that God’s timing is part of His will, and that the believer who runs ahead of it, even towards a good thing, is not obeying. Waiting is not wasted time. It is the place where faith is tested and character formed. It teaches patience, it purifies motives, and it throws the heart back onto God as its only sure possession.

The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD. LAMENTATIONS 3:25–26

She returned to these themes in Quest for Love, published in 1996, which gathers the stories of other men and women and how they sought, or waited for, or gave up, love in obedience to God. Some of them married; some did not. The point of the book, as of its predecessor, is that the outcome is God’s business, and the obedience is ours.

Weighing it

Passion and Purity has helped a great many people, and its central teaching — that love belongs under the lordship of Christ, and that sexual intimacy belongs within marriage — is plainly scriptural. Three cautions are worth carrying.

The first concerns its particular counsel about men and women. She held that it is the man’s place to take the initiative in a relationship and the woman’s to wait and respond. Many Christians share that view; others, equally faithful, regard it as a matter of custom rather than command, and note that Scripture gives no single pattern for how marriages begin. Readers should weigh it accordingly. The larger question of her teaching on men and women is taken up in chapter eleven.

The second concerns the length of the waiting. Her story is an unusual one, shaped by Jim’s particular uncertainty and by their particular calling. It should not be turned into a rule that long uncertainty is a mark of godliness. Some Christians are rightly sure much sooner.

The third concerns those for whom the waiting does not end in marriage. A book about a courtship that finished at the altar can leave single readers feeling that the story is not for them. She knew this, and her later writing on loneliness and singleness tried to answer it. The promise of Psalm 37 is not that God will give us the person we desire, but that He will give us Himself, and with Himself the desires He has placed in us, fulfilled in His way and in His time.

But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. MATTHEW 6:33
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Is there a desire for love, marriage or companionship that you have never fully placed under Christ’s lordship? Name it, and offer it to Him today.

2. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8, and ask honestly whether your conduct and your imagination honour God.

3. If you are waiting for something good that has not come, consider what God may be forming in you in the waiting.

4. If you are married, thank God for the way He brought you together, and pray for a young person you know who is waiting.

5. If you are single, read Psalm 16 and give thanks that the Lord is the portion of your inheritance.

A PRAYER
Lord, You made us for love, and You know the strength of the desires You have put in us.
I bring You my heart and my hopes, and I lay them on the altar. Do with them as You will.
Keep me pure in body and in mind. Keep me from running ahead of You, and teach me to wait quietly for Your time.
Whether You give me what I long for or give me Yourself instead, let me find my delight in You, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Loneliness
fields.body_html:
I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top. PSALM 102:7

Few Christian writers of the twentieth century had more right to speak about being alone than Elisabeth Elliot. She waited five years, much of it apart, for a man who was not sure he would ever marry. She went to Ecuador as a single woman. She was a widow at twenty-nine, with a daughter not yet a year old, in a jungle station far from her family. She lived for a time among a people whose language she was still learning and whose ways were not her own, in a household where relations were strained. She married again and was widowed again within five years. For most of her adult life, in one way or another, she knew what it was to come home to an empty room.

In 1988 she gathered what she had learned into a short book called simply Loneliness. It was later reissued under the title The Path of Loneliness, and the longer title says something about its argument. Loneliness, for her, was not a dead end. It was a road, and the question was where it led.

Not a sin, and not a disease

The first thing the book does is to take loneliness seriously. She did not treat it as a failure of faith, as though a believer who felt alone must be doing something wrong. Nor did she treat it as a problem to be solved by the right technique, a busier diary or a better social life. It is, in her account, one of the real sufferings of a fallen world, felt by the widow and the single, but also by the married, the elderly, the sick, the newcomer, the missionary, the leader who must decide alone, and the believer who has simply been misunderstood. Scripture is full of it. The psalmist compares himself to a sparrow alone on a roof. Elijah lies down under a juniper tree and asks to die. Paul at his first defence finds that every man has deserted him.

At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge. Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me. 2 TIMOTHY 4:16–17

And above all there is the Lord Himself, forsaken by His friends in the garden and crying out on the cross. The Christian who is lonely is not walking a road that Christ has not walked first. That, for her, was the beginning of comfort: not an explanation, but company.

Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me. JOHN 16:32

The wilderness

The governing picture of the book is the wilderness. In Scripture the wilderness is a hard place — dry, lonely and dangerous — but it is also the place where God meets His people. Israel was led there and fed there. Moses was sent there before he was sent to Pharaoh. Elijah was fed there by ravens and by an angel. John the Baptist was formed there, and the Lord Himself was driven there by the Spirit before His ministry began. The prophet Hosea even pictures God leading His unfaithful people into the wilderness on purpose, in order to speak to them tenderly.

Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her. HOSEA 2:14

Her counsel, in substance, was that the lonely believer should not spend all his strength trying to get out of the wilderness, but should ask what God means to say to him in it. That does not mean refusing help, or friendship, or marriage if it is given. It means refusing to treat loneliness as the worst thing that can happen, and refusing to grasp at whatever will dull it. She was frank that many people try to fill the empty place with things that cannot fill it — compulsive busyness, entertainment, food, a hurried relationship, self-pity nursed in private — and that these leave the heart lonelier than before.

Accept, and offer

The practical heart of the book is the same pattern that runs through all her teaching, and which chapter six of this companion has already traced: receive what God gives, and give it back to Him. Loneliness, she taught, is to be accepted as part of the life God has assigned for now — not resented, not denied, not dressed up as something else. It is then to be offered to Him, as one would offer any other gift. The widow’s empty evenings, the single woman’s unshared table, the unanswered letter, the ache at a wedding: these can be laid in the hands of Christ as a sacrifice, and in His hands they become something other than a wound.

God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land. PSALM 68:6

This was not, in her telling, a trick for making the feeling go away. Sometimes it does not go away. But the offering changes what the loneliness is for. Instead of being a hole in the middle of life, it becomes a place of meeting with God and a source of usefulness to others. She urged the lonely, again and again, to turn outward — to look for someone else who is alone and to do something for them. The person who has been comforted in the wilderness has something to give.

Singleness and widowhood

Two particular kinds of loneliness run through the book, and through her other writing too. The first is singleness. She held, with the apostle Paul, that the unmarried life is not a lesser life or a waiting room, but a calling in which a person may be wholly given to the Lord. She did not pretend it was easy, and she knew from her own long wait how strong the longing for marriage can be. But she insisted that a single person’s life belongs to God as fully as a married person’s, and that it is to be lived now, not postponed until a wedding that may never come.

But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:32

The second is widowhood. She wrote of it from inside, and twice over. She did not romanticise grief, and she did not hurry the widow towards cheerfulness. But she did insist that the God who had taken a husband had not withdrawn Himself, and that Scripture’s promises to the widow are not decorations. God calls Himself her husband and her defender. He has not stopped being either.

For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called. ISAIAH 54:5

Weighing it

There is much here that is simply wise and simply scriptural, and many lonely readers have found the book a steady friend. Two cautions may be worth carrying.

The first is that her own temperament was unusually self-contained. She was reserved by nature and disciplined by habit, and some readers find her counsel to accept and offer loneliness bracing to the point of austerity. They should remember that the same Scripture which tells us to bear our burdens also tells the church to bear one another’s. Her teaching does not let the church off the hook. The lonely are to offer their solitude to God; the rest of us are to set the solitary in families, by an open door and a laid place at the table.

The second is that loneliness sometimes has causes that need more than spiritual counsel — depression, illness, isolation that could be remedied by practical help. Nothing in her teaching forbids seeking that help, and she would not have wanted it read that way. Acceptance is not the same as passivity. It is the refusal to rebel against what God has given, joined with every lawful effort to do the next thing well.

And the LORD, he it is that doth go before thee; he will be with thee, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee: fear not, neither be dismayed. DEUTERONOMY 31:8
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the kind of loneliness you know best — singleness, widowhood, distance, misunderstanding, leadership, age. Tell God about it plainly, without dressing it up.

2. Ask what you have been using to fill the empty place. Is it filling it, or only dulling it?

3. Read Hosea 2:14–15. What might God want to say to you in the wilderness that He could not say elsewhere?

4. Offer your loneliness to God today in a short, specific prayer, as you would offer a gift.

5. Think of one person who is alone this week. Invite them to your table, or write to them, before the week is out.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were left alone by Your friends, and yet You were not alone, because the Father was with You.
You know the empty places in my life, the evenings no one shares and the burdens no one sees. I do not hide them from You.
I accept the life You have given me for now, and I offer You its loneliness. Take it, and make it a place where I meet You.
Make me a friend to the lonely, and set the solitary in families through me, for Your name’s sake. Amen.

fields.body_html:
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. GENESIS 1:27

No part of Elisabeth Elliot’s teaching has been more loved, or more argued over, than what she said about being a woman. She said it in many places — in conference talks, in her newsletter, on the radio — but she said it most fully in a short book published in 1976, Let Me Be a Woman. She wrote it for her daughter Valerie, who was about to be married, as a series of brief chapters on singleness, marriage and womanhood, and it has been given by mothers to daughters ever since. Five years later she wrote a companion for young men, The Mark of a Man, adapted from letters to her nephew Pete. This chapter sets out the teaching of the two books as fairly as it can, and then notes, as honestly, where faithful Christians have disagreed.

Given, not chosen

The foundation of her argument was creation. A human being is made male or female by God, and that is not an accident of biology or a role assigned by culture, but part of what he or she has been given. Her deepest objection to much of the thinking of her day was that it treated sex as a thing to be overcome or redefined, rather than a gift to be received. For her, as for all her teaching, the Christian’s first response to what God has given is acceptance. A woman is not to apologise for being a woman, nor to measure her worth by how closely she can resemble a man. She is to ask what God meant by making her as she is, and to give herself gladly to that.

Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture. PSALM 100:3

She did not mean that every woman must marry, or that a woman’s whole calling is the home. She had been single for years, a translator, a missionary, a widow, and later a teacher and writer with a public ministry. Let Me Be a Woman gives a good deal of attention to the single woman, and insists that she is no less a woman for being unmarried.

Order and submission

The more contested part of her teaching concerned marriage. Following the apostle Paul in Ephesians 5, she taught that marriage is meant to be a picture of Christ and His church, and that the picture has an order in it: the husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, and the wife is to submit to her husband as the church submits to Christ. She saw this order as part of a larger pattern running through creation, in which God has arranged things in a hierarchy not of value but of function, and in which even the Son, equal with the Father, delights to do the Father’s will.

Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. EPHESIANS 5:22
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. EPHESIANS 5:25

Three things are worth noticing about how she presented it. First, she held that submission is something a wife gives, freely, not something a husband extracts; it is an offering made to the Lord, of a piece with every other offering in her teaching. Second, she held that it implies nothing about a woman’s worth or intelligence, and she had no patience with men who thought otherwise. Third, she held that the husband’s calling is the heavier of the two, because the pattern he is to follow is a Saviour who died. Headship in her account is not privilege but responsibility, and its shape is the cross.

A model she held up for women was Mary of Nazareth, who heard the word of God and answered that she was the Lord’s handmaid. In her account that reply showed what a woman’s calling looks like at its best, and indeed what Christian discipleship looks like in any form: a glad yes to what God asks.

And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. LUKE 1:38

The Mark of a Man

The Mark of a Man approaches the same subject from the other side. Written for a young man, it calls him to the masculine virtues as she understood them — taking responsibility, protecting and providing, leading by serving, showing courage and initiative, keeping his word, forgiving, enduring. Its model is Christ, who did not grasp at His rights but took the form of a servant. She was as hard on passive, self-indulgent men as on anyone, and the book is in many ways a summons to young men to grow up.

Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. 1 CORINTHIANS 16:13
Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men. PHILIPPIANS 2:5–7

Where Christians differ

It would be dishonest to present this teaching as though all believers accept it. Many do. A large number of evangelical Christians, sometimes called complementarians, hold views close to hers, and her books did much to shape that position. But other evangelicals, sometimes called egalitarians, read the same Scriptures differently. They point to Paul’s call to mutual submission in the verse just before the instruction to wives, to his statement that in Christ there is neither male nor female, to the women who laboured with him in the gospel, and to the way the New Testament household codes may address the culture of their day. They hold that marriage should be a partnership without a fixed order of authority, and that the gifts of the Spirit, not sex, should determine roles in the church.

Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. EPHESIANS 5:21
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. GALATIANS 3:28

Some critics have also felt that her portrait of femininity carried the stamp of mid-century American culture as much as of Scripture, or noted the tension between her teaching and her own life of independent work and public speaking — a tension she was aware of and addressed in her own way. Others have feared that teaching on submission can be misused by domineering husbands. She did not teach that a wife must follow her husband into sin, and her insistence on the husband’s self-giving love was meant to exclude tyranny; Christians on every side of the debate would add that no reading of these texts can require anyone to remain under abuse.

This companion does not settle the question. Faithful Christians who love the Bible hold both views, and the debate turns on careful reading of particular texts. What can be said is that her teaching was not a slogan. It came from a woman who had obeyed God at great cost, who asked at least as much of men as of women, and who grounded everything in the self-giving love of Christ. Readers on both sides can learn from that, and should weigh her conclusions where they belong, under Scripture.

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. ACTS 17:11
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Do you receive your being a man or a woman as a gift from God, or as something to manage or resent? Thank God for how He made you.

2. Read Ephesians 5:21–33 slowly. What does it ask of a husband, and what of a wife? Which part do you find hardest?

3. If you are married, ask how your marriage could show more clearly the self-giving love of Christ. Begin with your own part, not your spouse’s.

4. If you hold a different view from hers, state her argument fairly to yourself before you answer it. If you share it, ask how it might be misused, and guard against that.

5. Like Mary, say yes to one thing God is asking of you this week.

Lord God, You made us male and female in Your image, and You called it very good.
Teach me to receive the way You made me with thanksgiving, and to give myself gladly to Your purpose for my life.
Where I am proud, humble me. Where I grasp at rights, make me like Christ, who took the form of a servant.
Give us grace, where we differ, to search the Scriptures together in love. And make every Christian home a picture of Your Son and His church. Amen.

fields.title: The Shaping of a Christian Home
fields.body_html:
Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. PSALM 127:1

In 1992, when she was in her sixties, Elisabeth Elliot published a book about the house she grew up in. The Shaping of a Christian Family is partly a memoir and partly a book of counsel. It describes the home of Philip and Katharine Howard — first in Germantown, in Philadelphia, and then in Moorestown, New Jersey, with summers in the hills of New Hampshire — where six children were raised on Scripture, hymns, order and prayer. She wrote it, in part, because she believed that the ordinary disciplines of a Christian home were being forgotten. It is one of the warmest of her books.

A house ordered by Scripture

The Howards’ home was not elaborate. Her father edited a Christian weekly. But the house had a shape, and the shape was given by the Word of God. There were times for meals and times for work, times for bed and times for getting up, and the children were expected to keep them. There was family worship each day, at which the Bible was read, a hymn was sung and the family prayed together. The children memorised Scripture and learned the great hymns of the church verse by verse, so that by the time they were grown they carried a store of both in their heads. She believed that this storehouse had served her well in the jungle, in grief and in old age, when there was no book at hand and no one to pray with.

And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. DEUTERONOMY 6:6–7

This is the first lesson of the book: that faith is passed on less by occasional effort than by daily habit. A child learns what matters to his parents by watching what they actually do every day. If the Bible is opened every morning, the child learns that it matters. If prayer is a matter of course, the child learns that God is near. Nothing in the book suggests that habits save anyone. But habits make room, and God is pleased to work in the room they make.

Hymns and the memory

She gave special attention to hymn-singing, and it is worth pausing on it. The hymns sung in the Howard home were, for the most part, the older hymns of the church, with their doctrine, their Scripture and their many verses. Learned in childhood, they became a lifelong theology. She found, again and again, that a line from a hymn came back to her when she most needed it. One she often recalled was How Firm a Foundation, with its promise from God to the believer passing through deep waters: “The rivers of woe shall not thee overflow.”

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. COLOSSIANS 3:16

The counsel for families today is simple and practical. Sing together. Choose hymns with something in them. Sing all the verses. Let children learn them by heart before they can understand them, as they learn so much else. The understanding will come.

Discipline and courtesy

The book is honest that the Howard home was strict. Disobedience was corrected, sometimes firmly. Children were expected to be courteous and to do their share of the work. She did not defend this as a matter of temperament but as a matter of love: parents who do not correct their children, she believed, are not kinder than those who do, only lazier. The aim of discipline was not to break a child but to train him, so that obedience to parents might become the school of obedience to God.

And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. EPHESIANS 6:4

She was equally insistent that order is not the same as coldness. She described a home in which the children knew they were loved, in which their parents’ marriage was visibly happy, and in which laughter and music and the beauty of the outdoors had their place. The long summers at the family cottage in Franconia belong to the picture as much as the rules.

An open door

One feature of the house seems to have made a particular impression on her. It was hospitable. Missionaries on furlough, visiting preachers, students and strangers sat at the Howards’ table, and the children grew up hearing of the work of God in many countries from the people doing it. Their world was larger than their town. It is not hard to see a connection between that open table and the fact that more than one of the six children went on into Christian work in other lands.

Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. HEBREWS 13:2

Hospitality, in her teaching, did not require money or a large house. It required a willingness to let others into ordinary life — to set another place, to share what there was, to let guests see the family as it really was. It is one of the simplest ways in which a Christian home can serve the church and the world.

Weighing it

The book can be read in two ways, and only one of them is right. It can be read as a formula — do these things, and your children will turn out well. That reading is mistaken, and she did not intend it. No method guarantees faith; children raised in godly homes sometimes wander, and children from chaotic homes are sometimes found by God. Parents who have done their best and grieve over a child should not take this book as an accusation.

The better reading takes it as a testimony and a stirring. Here is what one family did, by God’s grace, with very ordinary means. Some of its customs belong to its time and place. Its principles do not: that the Word of God should be at the centre of a home, that faith is learned by daily habit, that love and order are friends, and that the door should be open.

When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also. 2 TIMOTHY 1:5
But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. JOSHUA 24:15
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of the home you grew up in. Give thanks for what was good in it, and bring to God what was not.

2. If you have a household, choose one daily habit of Scripture or prayer that you could keep together, and begin it this week, however small.

3. Choose one hymn with real substance in it. Learn all its verses, and teach it to a child.

4. Ask whether your home has order without love, or love without order. Pray for what is lacking.

5. Set an extra place at your table this month for someone who would not otherwise be invited.

A PRAYER
Lord, unless You build the house, we labour in vain. Build ours.
Put Your Word at the centre of our days, and make our habits a room where You are pleased to work.
Give us love that corrects and order that is kind. Give our children hearts that know You for themselves.
Open our doors to the stranger and the weary, and let our homes be places where others meet You. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Amen.

fields.title: No Graven Image
fields.body_html:
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. EXODUS 20:4

In 1966 Elisabeth Elliot published a novel. It was the only one she ever wrote, and it troubled many of the readers who had loved Through Gates of Splendor. Then Pedro falls ill, she gives him an injection of penicillin, and he dies of a violent reaction to it. The book does not end with a vindication. It ends with a missionary stripped of her success story and left with God.

The novel is fiction, but it was not invented out of nothing. It drew on what she had lived through, and it put into story form a conviction that runs through the whole of her teaching. God is not a means to our ends. He is not a guarantor of missionary results, or of happy endings, or of the kind of meaning we would choose. He is God, and He may not be fashioned into an image of what we want Him to be.

Where my work has come to ashes, give me beauty in Your time. Where it never comes in this life, keep me trusting You still.
Make me faithful to plant and water, and leave the increase to You. Though You slay me, yet will I trust in You. Amen.

fields.title: A Chance to Die
fields.body_html:
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. JOHN 12:24

Of all the Christians who shaped Elisabeth Elliot, none mattered more to her than Amy Carmichael. She had read her since she was young, absorbed her poems and her prose, and spoke of her for the rest of her life as one of her chief teachers in the way of the cross. In 1987 she paid the debt in a full-length biography, A Chance to Die: The Life and Legacy of Amy Carmichael. It is one of her best books, and it is as much a book about discipleship as a biography. To understand what Elisabeth Elliot taught about the death of self, it is the place to go.

The woman she wrote about

Amy Carmichael was born in 1867 in the village of Millisle, in the north of Ireland. As a young woman she came under the influence of the Keswick movement, with its call to a life wholly surrendered to Christ, and she felt called to missionary work. After a brief and difficult time in Japan she went to South India in 1895, and she never came home. In the Tinnevelly district she gathered a band of Indian women who travelled with her through the villages, and she began to learn of the children, especially girls, who were given to the temples. She gave the rest of her life to rescuing such children and to raising them in Christ. The community that grew up around her became known as the Dohnavur Fellowship. In 1931 a fall left her injured, and for the last twenty years of her life she was largely confined to her room, from which she wrote many of the books that are still read today. She died in 1951.

Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God. MARK 10:14

The cross at the centre

What drew Elisabeth Elliot to her was not chiefly the romance of her work, though it was romantic enough. It was her understanding of the Christian life as a life laid down. Amy Carmichael believed that the call of Christ is a call to die — to one’s own preferences, one’s own reputation, one’s own comfort and one’s own plans — so that the life of Jesus may be seen in the believer. The title of the biography is said to come from her own description of missionary life as, in effect, a chance to die. Elisabeth Elliot made that the key to the whole story.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. LUKE 9:23

This is not a morbid idea, though it can sound like one. It is the teaching of the Lord Himself, who said that the grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die if it is to bear fruit. The death in question is not of the body, but of the self that wants its own way. And the purpose is not loss but life: the fruit that comes only from a life given away.

Amy Carmichael put this into a small book of searching sentences, If, which is in the Ochorus library. Each sentence describes a failure of love and ends with the confession that one who fails in this way knows nothing of Calvary love. One of them, in the library’s text, reads: “If I cling to choices simply because they are my choices; if I give any room to personal likes and dislikes, then I know nothing of Calvary love.” It is the kind of mirror in which no one looks comfortably.

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. GALATIANS 2:20

Honesty about the work

There was a second reason for her admiration. Amy Carmichael told the truth about missionary work. Her early book Things as They Are, also in the Ochorus library, described the spiritual darkness of the villages and the slow, often discouraging labour of the missionaries without the cheerful gloss that supporters at home expected. Some at home did not want to hear it. Elisabeth Elliot, who had made the same refusal in her own telling of Ecuador, saw in Amy a fellow witness to the truth that God’s work is done through weakness, failure and long waiting, and not only through visible success.

For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:11

Not a plaster saint

A Chance to Die is not hagiography, and that is part of its value. Elisabeth Elliot admired Amy Carmichael more than almost anyone, but she did not hide her strong will, her decided opinions, the severity of some of her standards or the frictions that some of her decisions caused with others. She showed a woman who had to die to herself daily precisely because her self was so strong. That honesty makes the book more useful, not less. The way of the cross is not for people who have no self to lose. It is for people like us.

The last twenty years of Amy Carmichael’s life also mattered to her. A woman who had been constantly active was laid aside, unable to travel or to work as she had, and she had to learn a different kind of death: the surrender of usefulness itself. Out of that confinement came much of her best writing. Elisabeth Elliot, who would herself be laid aside in her last years, saw in it the truth that God’s strength is made perfect in weakness, and that a life can bear fruit long after it has stopped being busy.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 CORINTHIANS 12:9

Weighing it

The teaching on the death of self needs one guard. It can be heard as a call to self-hatred, or to a grim suppression of every desire, or to a kind of spiritual performance in which the believer measures his holiness by how much he has given up. That is not what Scripture means, and not what either woman meant at her best. The self that dies is the self that sets itself against God. What rises in its place is not a blank but a person made new, free to love because no longer bound to self. The cross is always followed by the resurrection.

Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. ROMANS 6:4
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Luke 9:23–25. What in your life would it mean to take up your cross today, specifically?

2. Name one preference, one plan or one part of your reputation that you are clinging to. Lay it down before God.

3. Read Amy Carmichael’s If in the Ochorus library, a few sentences at a time. Stop at the one that troubles you most and pray over it.

4. If you have been laid aside by illness or age, ask God what fruit He may intend from this season, and offer it to Him.

5. Obtain A Chance to Die and read the life for yourself, watching for the moments when Amy chose the way of the cross.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You fell into the ground and died, that You might bring forth much fruit.
I confess how tightly I hold my own choices, my own comfort and my own good name.
Teach me to take up my cross daily and follow You. Let the self that sets itself against You die, and let Your life be seen in me.
Make me fruitful in action or in weakness, as You choose, and let me walk in newness of life. Amen.

fields.title: Keep a Quiet Heart
fields.body_html:
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not. ISAIAH 30:15

In 1995 Elisabeth Elliot gathered a selection of the short pieces she had written for her newsletter into a book called Keep a Quiet Heart. It is not a treatise. It is a collection of brief readings, many only a page or two long, on a wide range of subjects, from prayer and grief to the small duties and irritations of ordinary days. But a single concern holds it together, and the title names it. The Christian is called to a quiet heart — not an empty heart, nor an untroubled life, but an inner stillness that rests in God while the world outside goes on changing. Chapter four of this companion has drawn from the same book her counsel to do the next thing. This chapter takes up its teaching on anxiety, trust and peace.

The noise inside

Most of what disturbs us, she observed, comes not from what is happening but from what we fear may happen. The heart runs ahead into tomorrow, rehearses conversations that have not taken place, imagines losses that have not come, and tries to carry burdens that God has not yet laid on it. That restless running ahead is what Scripture calls anxiety, or in the old English of the King James Bible, being careful. The Lord forbids it, not because the future does not matter, but because it is not ours to carry.

Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment? MATTHEW 6:25

Her remedy was not a technique of relaxation but a turning of attention. The anxious heart is a heart fixed on itself and its circumstances. The quiet heart is a heart fixed on God. Isaiah promised perfect peace to the one whose mind is stayed on the Lord, and she took the promise at its word. Peace is not found by solving every problem; it is found by trusting the One who is in charge of them.

Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. ISAIAH 26:3

Prayer with thanksgiving

A passage she returned to often on this subject was Paul’s word to the Philippians. Be anxious for nothing; in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, make your requests known to God; and the peace of God will guard your heart and mind. She noticed that the promise is not that God will grant every request. It is that His peace will keep the heart. And she noticed the little phrase in the middle: with thanksgiving. The anxious person asks with clenched hands. The trusting person asks with open ones, already thanking God for who He is, whatever He decides.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 4:6–7

In practice this meant, for her, that every worry should be turned into a prayer as soon as it is noticed, and then left with God. If the worry returns, it should be given back again. She did not pretend that this was easy, or that a person who has once handed over a care will never pick it up again. But she held that the habit can be learned, and that it grows stronger with use.

Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. 1 PETER 5:7

Quiet amid change

fields.title: On Asking God Why
fields.body_html:
O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save! HABAKKUK 1:2

Every Christian who suffers asks the question sooner or later. Why this? Why me? Why now? Why did He not prevent it? Elisabeth Elliot had more reason than most to ask it, and she did not pretend otherwise. In 1989 she published a collection of short essays under the title On Asking God Why, and the book, together with much else she wrote, sets out how she came to think about the question. Her answer was not that the question is forbidden. It was that the answer, when it comes, is usually not an explanation but a Person.

The question is allowed

She began, in substance, by defending the question. Scripture is full of it. Job asks why he was ever born. The psalmists ask why God has forsaken them, why the wicked prosper, why He hides His face. Habakkuk asks why God makes him look upon injustice. And on the cross the Lord Jesus Himself cried out, in the words of the twenty-second Psalm, asking why His God had forsaken Him. A faith that cannot ask why is not stronger than a faith that can. It is only less honest.

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? MATTHEW 27:46

But she drew a distinction between two ways of asking. There is the why of a child who trusts his father and wants to understand, and there is the why of a rebel who demands that God justify Himself before he will obey. The first is a prayer. The second is an accusation. The same words can carry either, and the difference lies in the heart.

Job’s answer

The book of Job was central to her thinking here, as it has been for many who suffer. Job asks why, at length and with great bitterness. His friends offer answers, all of them neat and most of them wrong. When God at last speaks, He does not explain the wager in heaven or the reasons for Job’s losses. He asks Job questions instead — about the foundations of the earth, the storehouses of the snow, the wild goat and the war horse — and in the asking He shows Job Himself. Job is not given an explanation. He is given God. And he is satisfied.

Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding. JOB 38:4
I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. JOB 42:5

That, for her, was the pattern. God does not owe us explanations, and He seldom gives them. What He gives is Himself — His presence, His character, His promises — and that turns out to be enough, in a way that an explanation would never be. An explanation, even if we could understand it, would not hold us up in the dark. A Father’s hand will.

The secret things

She drew comfort from the verse in Deuteronomy which divides what God has kept from what He has given. The secret things belong to the Lord. The revealed things belong to us, so that we may do them. Much of the agony of asking why comes from demanding the secret things. Much of the peace that follows comes from turning to the revealed things — what God has plainly said, and what He has plainly asked us to do next.

The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law. DEUTERONOMY 29:29

This is where her teaching on suffering and her teaching on duty meet. When the question has no answer, the believer is not left with nothing. He is left with the next thing God has given him to do, and with the promise that God is working all things together for good. That promise does not say that all things are good. It says that God is at work in them for the good of those who love Him, which is a different and greater thing.

And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. ROMANS 8:28

Hereafter

She also held, with the whole Christian tradition, that some answers are only postponed. When the Lord washed His disciples’ feet and Peter protested, Jesus told him that he did not understand now but would understand afterwards. There are things we will see only from the other side. That is not an evasion. It is a promise that the story is not yet finished, and that the Author knows how it ends.

Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter. JOHN 13:7
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! ROMANS 11:33

Weighing it

This teaching is faithful to Scripture, and especially to Job, and it has helped many through the darkest times of their lives. Two cautions are worth noting.

The first is that it can be misused by comforters. To tell a grieving person that God does not owe them an explanation is true; to tell them so too quickly is cruel. Job’s friends were wrong not only in their theology but in their timing and their tone. The Lord wept at the grave of Lazarus before He raised him. The right response to someone asking why is usually to weep with them first, and to speak of God’s sovereignty later, if at all.

Jesus wept. JOHN 11:35

The second is that her answer — that God gives Himself rather than reasons — is an answer for faith, not a proof for the sceptic. It satisfied Job because Job already knew whom he was dealing with. For the believer that is enough. For the unbeliever, the place to begin is not with the why of suffering but with the cross, where God Himself entered our suffering and answered the deepest why of all.

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. HABAKKUK 3:17–18
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. What is the why you have been asking God? Write it down honestly.

2. Examine how you have been asking it — as a child seeking to understand, or as one demanding that God justify Himself.

3. Read Job 38–42 in one sitting. Notice what God says, and what He does not say.

4. Separate the secret things from the revealed things in your situation. What has God plainly asked you to do next? Do it.

5. When someone near you asks why, weep with them before you speak. Pray for the grace to know when to be silent.

A PRAYER
Lord, You heard Job’s questions and Habakkuk’s complaint, and You heard Your own Son cry out on the cross. Hear mine.
I do not understand what You are doing. I ask You why, and I ask as Your child.
If You do not give me reasons, give me Yourself. Let me hear of You no longer by the hearing of the ear, but see You.
Keep the secret things, and help me to do the revealed ones. And though the fig tree does not blossom, let me rejoice in You. Amen.

fields.title: Gratitude in All Things
fields.body_html:
In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:18

From 1988 to 2001 Elisabeth Elliot spoke to a large listening audience through a weekday radio programme called Gateway to Joy. The name suited her teaching. She believed that the gate through which joy enters a human life is not good fortune but thanksgiving — and that thanksgiving is open to anyone, in any circumstance, because it rests not on what happens to us but on who God is. Gratitude ran through her teaching like a bright thread. It was, for her, not an emotion to be waited for but a habit of faith to be practised.

In everything, not for everything

She was careful with Paul’s command to the Thessalonians. It says to give thanks in everything, and she did not take it to mean that we must thank God for evil as though evil were good. A murder, a betrayal, a cancer, a death are not gifts in themselves. But in every one of them there is something to give thanks for: that God is present, that He has not changed, that He is able to bring good out of what He did not cause, that the sufferer is not abandoned, that Christ has gone this way before. The believer may thank God in the darkness without pretending that the darkness is light.

Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. EPHESIANS 5:20

Ephesians goes further and speaks of giving thanks for all things, and here she pointed to the larger picture of God’s sovereignty. If nothing reaches the believer except through the hands of a loving Father, then even what is painful comes wrapped, in the end, in His purpose. She did not use that truth to silence grief. She used it to steady faith.

Job’s blessing

The scriptural model she returned to was Job in the first hour of his losses, whose words of acceptance chapter six has already considered. Before any of the arguments, before the friends came, he fell to the ground and worshipped. That act of worship did not take away his grief. It came out of it. And it shows that thanksgiving is not the opposite of mourning but its companion in the believer’s heart.

Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped. JOB 1:20

Her own life gave her the right to teach this. She had been bereaved twice, had lost her work more than once, and knew the long weariness of disappointment. She did not teach thanksgiving from a comfortable chair. She taught it as something she had to choose, often against her feelings, and found to be true.

The sacrifice of praise

The letter to the Hebrews speaks of the sacrifice of praise, and the word sacrifice mattered in her teaching. A sacrifice costs something. Praise that springs up naturally when all is well costs nothing; praise offered in loss is an offering laid on the altar. It belongs with all the other offerings in her teaching — of loneliness, of suffering, of plans and preferences — and like them it is transformed in God’s hands. The believer who gives thanks when it is hardest often finds that the giving changes him.

By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. HEBREWS 13:15

Everlasting love

The two promises with which Gateway to Joy began, as chapter three described — the everlasting love and the everlasting arms — explain her gratitude. Thanksgiving is the natural response of someone who believes them. If God’s love is everlasting, nothing can exhaust it; if His arms are underneath, nothing can let us fall below them. Joy, in her teaching, did not wait for sorrow to be taken away; it came from God’s being near, and gratitude is the way the heart turns towards Him.

Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. PSALM 16:11

Ordinary gifts

Not all her teaching on gratitude was about suffering. Much of it was about the ordinary goods of life that most of us take for granted: food, work, a home, the faces of friends, the beauty of the sea and the sky, the morning. She thought that ingratitude for small things is one of the commonest sins of comfortable Christians, and that it quietly poisons the heart. The cure is simple and old: to stop and say thank you, to God and to others, for every gift, however small. She thought a grateful household a happy one, and saying thank you a habit worth teaching to every child.

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. JAMES 1:17
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits. PSALM 103:2

Weighing it

This teaching is close to the centre of the New Testament, and it needs little qualification. One caution may help. Gratitude in all things can be demanded of others in a way that wounds — as though a grieving person who does not feel thankful were failing God. The command is given to each believer for himself. We may encourage one another in it, but gently, and we should be quicker to give thanks for our own sorrows than to require others to give thanks for theirs. The psalms of lament stand in the same Bible as the psalms of praise, and many of them move from one to the other in the course of a few verses. That movement is the path she was describing.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before you go to sleep tonight, name five specific things from the day for which you are grateful, and thank God for each.

2. Think of your present hardest circumstance. Find one thing in it, not about it, for which you can honestly give thanks.

3. Read Job 1:20–22. Pray Job’s words over something you have lost.

4. Write a thank-you letter this week to someone who has never been properly thanked.

5. Begin each day this week by thanking God for one gift before you ask Him for anything.

A PRAYER
Father of lights, every good and perfect gift has come from You, and I have taken so many for granted. Forgive me.
Teach me to give thanks in everything — not pretending that sorrow is joy, but trusting that You are present in it.
When I have lost what I loved, let me fall down and worship You, as Job did, and not turn away.
You have loved me with an everlasting love, and underneath are the everlasting arms. Let my life be a sacrifice of praise to You, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

The believer may thank God in the darkness without pretending that the darkness is light. Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. EPHESIANS 5:20 Ephesians goes further and speaks of giving thanks for all things, and here she pointed to the larger picture of God’s sovereignty. If nothing reaches the believer except through the hands of a loving Father, then even what is painful comes wrapped, in the end, in His purpose. She did not use that truth to silence grief. She used it to steady faith. Job’s blessing The scriptural model she returned to was Job in the first hour of his losses, whose words of acceptance chapter six has already considered. Before any of the arguments, before the friends came, he fell to the ground and worshipped. That act of worship did not take away his grief. It came out of it. And it shows that thanksgiving is not the opposite of mourning but its companion in the believer’s heart. Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped. JOB 1:20 Her own life gave her the right to teach this. She had been bereaved twice, had lost her work more than once, and knew the long weariness of disappointment. She did not teach thanksgiving from a comfortable chair. She taught it as something she had to choose, often against her feelings, and found to be true. The sacrifice of praise The letter to the Hebrews speaks of the sacrifice of praise, and the word sacrifice mattered in her teaching. A sacrifice costs something. Praise that springs up naturally when all is well costs nothing; praise offered in loss is an offering laid on the altar. It belongs with all the other offerings in her teaching — of loneliness, of suffering, of plans and preferences — and like them it is transformed in God’s hands. The believer who gives thanks when it is hardest often finds that the giving changes him. By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. HEBREWS 13:15 Everlasting love The two promises with which Gateway to Joy began, as chapter three described — the everlasting love and the everlasting arms — explain her gratitude. Thanksgiving is the natural response of someone who believes them. If God’s love is everlasting, nothing can exhaust it; if His arms are underneath, nothing can let us fall below them. Joy, in her teaching, did not wait for sorrow to be taken away; it came from God’s being near, and gratitude is the way the heart turns towards Him. Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. PSALM 16:11 Ordinary gifts Not all her teaching on gratitude was about suffering. Much of it was about the ordinary goods of life that most of us take for granted: food, work, a home, the faces of friends, the beauty of the sea and the sky, the morning. She thought that ingratitude for small things is one of the commonest sins of comfortable Christians, and that it quietly poisons the heart. The cure is simple and old: to stop and say thank you, to God and to others, for every gift, however small. She thought a grateful household a happy one, and saying thank you a habit worth teaching to every child. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. JAMES 1:17 Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits. PSALM 103:2 Weighing it This teaching is close to the centre of the New Testament, and it needs little qualification. One caution may help. Gratitude in all things can be demanded of others in a way that wounds — as though a grieving person who does not feel thankful were failing God. The command is given to each believer for himself. We may encourage one another in it, but gently, and we should be quicker to give thanks for our own sorrows than to require others to give thanks for theirs. The psalms of lament stand in the same Bible as the psalms of praise, and many of them move from one to the other in the course of a few verses. That movement is the path she was describing. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Before you go to sleep tonight, name five specific things from the day for which you are grateful, and thank God for each. 2. Think of your present hardest circumstance. Find one thing in it, not about it, for which you can honestly give thanks. 3. Read Job 1:20–22. Pray Job’s words over something you have lost. 4. Write a thank-you letter this week to someone who has never been properly thanked. 5. Begin each day this week by thanking God for one gift before you ask Him for anything. A PRAYER Father of lights, every good and perfect gift has come from You, and I have taken so many for granted. Forgive me. Teach me to give thanks in everything — not pretending that sorrow is joy, but trusting that You are present in it. When I have lost what I loved, let me fall down and worship You, as Job did, and not turn away. You have loved me with an everlasting love, and underneath are the everlasting arms. Let my life be a sacrifice of praise to You, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
As for God, his way is perfect: the word of the LORD is tried: he is a buckler to all those that trust in him. PSALM 18:30

We have covered a good deal of ground in these chapters — her life, God’s sovereignty, the next thing, suffering, acceptance and offering, obedience, discipline, love and purity, loneliness, womanhood, the Christian home, the idols of the mind, the way of the cross, the quiet heart, the question why, and gratitude. It would be easy to come away thinking that Elisabeth Elliot taught many things. In truth she taught one thing, from many angles, for nearly half a century. God is sovereign, and God is love. Because He is both, the believer can accept whatever He gives, obey whatever He commands, and offer everything back to Him.

One thread

Look back over the chapters and the thread is plain. Her teaching on suffering is that truth applied to pain. Her teaching on the next thing is that truth applied to an ordinary morning. Her teaching on discipline and obedience is that truth applied to the body, the mind, the diary and the will. Passion and Purity is that truth applied to desire; Loneliness to the empty room; Let Me Be a Woman to marriage; The Shaping of a Christian Family to the home. No Graven Image is that truth turned against our own images of God. A Chance to Die is that truth lived out in another woman’s life. Keep a Quiet Heart, On Asking God Why and her years of radio are that truth applied to fear, to questions and to praise.

For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

A teacher, weighed

We have tried to be honest. She could be stern, and some found her manner cool or her counsel austere. Her teaching on womanhood and submission is held by many faithful Christians and questioned by many others. Her refusal of tidy endings unsettled readers who wanted missionary stories to end in victory. Her strong temperament sometimes made acceptance sound easier than it is for gentler souls. None of this has been raised to diminish her. She would have insisted on it. She had no patience with hero-worship, least of all of herself, and she took pains to correct the legend that had grown up around her first husband’s death.

What stands, when all of that is weighed, is a body of teaching unusually close to Scripture and unusually tested by life. She did not teach acceptance from a sheltered place. She taught it as a widow, twice; as a missionary whose work had been stolen and set back again and again; and in the end as a woman whose mind was slowly failing. Her teaching was paid for.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

What to do with it

The danger for any reader of a book like this is that they will admire her and change nothing. She would have regarded that as a failure — hers, and theirs. So here is the plainest counsel this companion can give. Go back to the chapter that made you uncomfortable — not the one you enjoyed, but the one you would rather not read again. That is likely to be where God is at work. Take its points for reflection and act on them, slowly, one at a time. Then do the next thing.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

Two things to carry

Carry away, first, the everlasting arms. Every day of her radio ministry began with that promise, and it is the ground of everything else she taught. You can accept what God gives because His love for you is everlasting. You can obey Him because His arms are underneath. You can offer Him your losses because nothing laid in those hands is ever wasted.

Carry away, second, the offering. The single thing she asked of her readers, again and again, was that they would give back to God whatever He had given them — joys and sorrows, plans and disappointments, marriage and singleness, strength and weakness. She believed that nothing so offered is lost. In that she was simply repeating the teaching of the Lord, who said that the one who loses his life for His sake will find it.

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. MATTHEW 16:25

A last word about the woman

In her last years she could no longer write, speak or remember much of what she had taught. Her husband Lars cared for her at home in Magnolia until she died on 15 June 2015, aged eighty-eight. Some who loved her found that ending hard to understand: that the woman who had taught so many to trust God in suffering should herself lose the mind with which she had trusted. But it fitted her teaching better than any triumphant final chapter could have done. The everlasting arms do not depend on our remembering them. They hold us when we can no longer hold on.

And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. ISAIAH 46:4

The right response to her is not admiration but faith in the God she served.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Return to the chapter of this book that most troubled you. Read it again, and act this week on the first of its points.

2. Name one thing God has given you — a joy or a sorrow — that you have not yet offered back to Him. Offer it today.

3. Obtain one of her own books and begin reading it this month, beginning with the guide in the next chapter.

4. Ask what the next thing is that God has given you to do. Do it.

5. Pray for someone who is old, or failing, or no longer able to remember, and if you can, visit them.

A PRAYER
Lord God, Your way is perfect, and Your word is tried. You are a shield to all who trust in You.
Thank You for the servant whose teaching we have been considering, and for the many You have steadied through her.
Do not let me stop at admiring her. Teach me to accept what You give, to obey what You command, and to offer You everything.
When I am old, carry me. When I cannot hold on, hold me. You have loved me with an everlasting love, and underneath are the everlasting arms. Amen.
